notes: The poet as carpenter of words (West 2007 ch. 1; Watkins 1995 ch. 5; formula craft-words): Ved. vácāṃsi ... takṣam 'I have fashioned words (for him)', Av. vacas-tašti- 'fashioning of utterance' (a Gathic strophe), Gk ἐπέων ... τέκτονες 'carpenters of verses'. Both roots, *wekʷ-os 'word' (Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος) and *tetḱ- 'fashion' (takṣ-, taš-, τέκτων), are shared. Vedic takṣam is an aorist injunctive; the lexicon has only the present of *tetḱ-, used here. 'For him' (Ved. asmai) is interpolated.

Poetry as weaving (West 2007 ch. 1): Av. vaf- 'weave' > 'hymn' (Y. 28.3 ufiiānī 'I will hymn'), Gk ὑφαίνω with ὕμνον (Bacchylides), OE wordcræft wæf 'I wove word-craft'; all *(h₁)webʰ-. The lexicon offers only derived presents of the root; the thematic wébʰeti (as OE wefan) is used, gloss approximate. The object is not shared (Gk ὕμνος, OE wordcræft): 'words' (wékʷos) is interpolated. Ved. váy-/ūvuḥ 'weave' (RV 1.61.8) is another root and is not cited.

path: erratum:i 'go' also mapped to the pronoun *is

notes: The song sent on its way with the 3sg imperative of 'go': Ved. prá ... etu (RV 1.154.3 mánma, 7.34.1 manīṣā́, 7.66.1 stómaḥ naḥ 'our praise') and Gk ἴτω ἀοιδή (West 2007 ch. 1). etu = ἴτω (*h₁éytu). The subject is renewed in each tradition (stóma-, mánman-, ἀοιδή); 'word' (wékʷos) is interpolated, as are pró (Vedic only) and 'our' (Ved. naḥ).

The song flies (*peth₂-): RV 1.25.4 'forth fly my thoughts' (pátanti), Homer's ἔπεα πτερόεντα 'winged words', Aeschylus' prayer that 'flies forth' (ποτάσθω) (West 2007 ch. 1). The verb root is shared (Ved. pátanti, Gk πτερ-όεντα, ποτά-); 'words' is the Greek noun (ἔπεα), the Vedic has vímanyavaḥ 'thoughts', so wékʷos is marked interpolated. A neuter plural subject takes a singular verb. 'Forth' (pró) stands for Ved. párā (interpolated); 'my' for Ved. me.

Poetry as recall, root *men- (West 2007 ch. 1): the Sibyl's 'ancient tales ... that I remember' and 'I remember (ek man) the giants' (Vsp. 1–2, confirmed in the local Edda), the Beowulf thane 'mindful of songs' who 'remembered' (gemunde) a multitude of old stories (confirmed locally), the Muses who 'would recall' (μνησαίατο, confirmed in the treebank), and the Vedic poets who 'think out' a praise (manāmahe). ON man and OE gemunan are preterite-presents, continuing the perfect *memón- (memóne); the Greek and Vedic forms are other stems of the root, so the match is root-level. 'Old words' renders forn spjöll / eald-gesegena: sénos and wékʷos are interpolated.

'Givers of good things' (Benfey; West 2007 ch. 3): Gk θεοὶ δωτῆρες ἐάων (Od. 8.325, checked in AGDT: δωτῆρες nom. pl. in apposition to θεοί; Hes. Th. 46), Av. vohunąm dātārō of the Aməša Spəṇtas (Y. 65.12, checked in CAB; Vr. 11.12 is not in CAB and is no longer cited), Ved. dātā́ vásūnām (RV 8.51.5, of Indra, VedaWeb NOM SG + GEN PL, checked). Agent noun of *deh₃- with the genitive plural of *h₁wésu- 'good' used as a noun; the Greek ἐάων is the archaic genitive plural of ἐΰς. Revised after round 4: (1) the agent noun is now the suffix-accented *dh₃tḗr (pie-lex-dh3texr, now usable), the type of all three cited cells (oxytone δωτήρ, Ved. dātā́ with the genitive, Benveniste's type, Av. dātar-); the root-accented déh₃tōr (δώτωρ type) is attested only in δῶτορ ἐάων (Od. 8.335), which is not cited. (2) 'Gods' (deywós, the interpolated NP head; Gk θεοί is not cognate) is dropped, so the line is the secure head-plus-dependent phrase itself, as an np utterance. Number and case: nominative plural with the Greek and Avestan (δωτῆρες, dātārō); the Vedic has the singular dātā́ of one god. Order: Gk δωτῆρες ἑάων and Ved. dātā́ vásūnām have the head first, Av. vohunąm dātārō the genitive first. Builder (2026-10-25 targeted evidence refresh): pie-lex-dh3texr now receives exact evidence in Greek and Indo-Iranian. Editorial review and eval-grade decisions are retained unchanged.

english: We call the giver of good things.

plan.english: We call the giver of good things.

notes: The epithet 'giver of good things' as the object of invocation: RV 8.51.5 'who is our giver of goods (dātā́ vásūnām), that Indra we call (hūmahe)' and Od. 8.335 Hermes addressed as δῶτορ ἑάων (both checked). Y. 16.1 (dātārəm vohunąm, checked) is support only: there vohunąm agrees with dāmanąm and dātar- 'creator' is likely *dʰeh₁- (review). The verb follows the Vedic middle hūmahe 'we call' with ǵʰuHéyeti (the éye-present, Ved. hváyati; hūmahe is the root present of the same root): Vedic only, interpolated (round 1 used Avestan yazamaide 'we worship', which rested on Y. 16.1). Engine limit as in poetics-gifts-007: the parallel points to oxytone *dh₃-tér- (Ved. dātā́), but only the root-accented déh₃tōr is usable; Gk δώτωρ (8.335) is that type.

english: I heard: he gives no horses for songs; he gives a cow.

plan.english: I heard: he gives no horses for songs; he gives a cow.

notes: The 'inverse dānastuti' (Watkins 1995: 187): the Irish quatrain (ro-cúala ... eochu ar dúana ... bó: 'I have heard he gives no horses for poems ... a cow'), whose frame ro-cúala 'I have heard' is the exact cognate of Vedic śuśrava (*ḱuḱlowh₂a) in praise of generosity (RV 1.109.2, 5: áśravam 'I heard you give more plentifully'); horses and cows are the canonical gifts of the Vedic dānastuti (RV 1.126.2 a hundred horses, cows). Ved. áśvān / OIr eochu, gónām / bó. The aorist follows Vedic áśravam (the OIr is a perfect). 'Give' is interpolated: OIr do-beir is *bʰer-, Vedic has dā-; dédeh₃ti chosen. 'Songs' (OIr dúana) is interpolated with kéh₂nmn̥ 'song'. Morphology caveat (review): the engine's 1sg root aorist ḱlḗm applies Stang's law (*ḱléwm̥ > *ḱlḗm); no daughter supports it (Ved. áśravam points to *(é)ḱlewm̥), and the Irish ro-cúala is a perfect. The lexicon's perfect ḱeḱlówe is glossed 'to be heard', so it cannot be used for 'I have heard'.

'Make great fame for someone' (Watkins 1995 ch. 5; West 2007 ch. 10): in the dānastuti of RV 5.18.5 the poet asks Agni to make great fame (máhi śrávaḥ kṛdhi) for the patrons, and Penelope 'makes great fame for herself' (μέγα … κλέος αὐτῇ ποιεῖτ(αι), Od. 2.125–126); both checked locally. The noun phrase *méǵh₂ ḱléwos is secure and the frame (make + great fame + beneficiary) is shared, but the verb is renewed in Greek (ποιέω is not cognate), so *kʷer- (Ved. kṛdhi, root-aorist imperative) is Vedic only, interpolated. 'Them' stands for Ved. maghónām 'the patrons'. Round 1 also carried the Vedic relative clause 'who gave me horses' (Vedic only); it is dropped, and Il. 6.446 is replaced by the Greek passage that has the same frame.

Kuhn's equation śrávaḥ ákṣitam = κλέος ἄφθιτον (RV 1.9.7, Il. 9.413, both confirmed locally), here in the poet's request on behalf of his patrons (RV 1.9.7 'set on us ... imperishable fame') and in Ibycus' pledge to Polycrates that he will have κλέος ἄφθιτον through the poet's song (Watkins 1995: 70; West 2007 ch. 10). The verb dʰeh₁ (Ved. dhehi) and 'on us' (asmé, rendered by the dative enclitic) are Vedic only, interpolated; Vedic also has pṛthú and bṛhát, left out.

'Good fame' *h₁wésu ḱléwos: Av. vohu sravah- (Y. 30.10 vaŋhāu srauuahī, confirmed locally) and OIr fó chlú, beside the compounds Ved. suśrávas-, Gk εὐκλεής, OIr sochla (West 2007 ch. 10; Homer renews the phrase as κλέος ἐσθλόν). The wish form (optative of the copula with a dative of possession) is interpolated; Avestan has a locative 'in good fame'.

english: How shall I win the reward?

plan.english: How shall I win the reward?

notes: The poet's fee *misdʰó- (Benveniste; Watkins 1995: 71): Zarathustra asks how he shall win his reward (kaϑā mīždəm hanānī, Y. 44.18, checked in CAB), and Pindar 'will win' the Athenians' gratitude as his μισθός (Pyth. 1.75–77; not in local corpora). Only 'reward' is shared; the verb (Avestan aorist subjunctive hanānī, *senh₂- = Ved. san- 'win'; Pindar has ἀρέομαι) and 'how' (kʷíh₁ for kaϑā) are Avestan only, interpolated. Round 1 also had 'ten horses' (Avestan only: ten mares, a stallion and a camel); dropped to keep the interpolated frame small.

The suppliant's opening demand for a hearing: Gk κλῦθί μευ (Il. 1.37, checked) = Ved. śrudhī (RV 1.25.19 imáṃ me … śrudhī hávam, checked), both the root-aorist imperative *ḱlu-dʰí. Both have a genitive/dative enclitic of the 1st person, so the line has the enclitic *moy (= Ved. me, Gk μοι), now rendered as a dative ('give ear to me'); round 1 had the accusative *me. The Sibyl's 'hearing I ask' (hljóðs, *ḱleu-to-, Vǫluspá 1, checked) is a different formation, support only (West 2007 ch. 2).

Candidate from the Phase 8c reader study (docs/research/8c-results.md): an addition to a known formula, not a new formula, and unconfirmed by an expert. Known: 'hear me' (poetics-gifts-015; West 2007 ch. 8 pp. 316-317, Schmitt 1967 §§396-405), but with non-cognate objects. New: *ḱlew- governing the cognate object *wékʷos (Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος, the same neuter s-stem) with a 1sg possessor, of a god hearing the worshipper. All loci checked. Vedic: RV 10.66.11c áhir budhnyàḥ śr̥ṇavad vácāṃsi me, 'may the Serpent of the Deep hear my words'; the same formula in RV 1.145.3b and 10.65.13c (the latter a 3pl, support). Greek: Il. 16.236 = 14.234 ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες, 'you heard my word' (Achilles' prayer to Zeus; Hera to Sleep). The line follows the Vedic formula: śr̥ṇavat is the subjunctive of the nasal present *ḱl̥-néw- (Ved. śr̥ṇóti, cited by that lemma so the check can find it). So the verb is root-level against Greek ἔκλυες, the thematic aorist of the same root, and the head is not shared in one formation. Plural object and enclitic genitive *moy follow the Vedic (vácāṃsi me); Greek has the singular and the possessive adjective ἐμόν, which is root-level only. Not a parallel: Pind. I. 6.42-43, cited by 8c, where ἔπος is the object of αὔδασε and ἐμάν goes with ἀράν under the renewed verb ἄκουσας (checked in glaux). Alternative reconstruction: the root aorist *ḱléwt (Gk κλῦθι, Ved. śrudhí), which matches neither passage's formation.
